title: A State Can't Cancel a Paid-Up Land Sale After a Change of Government: Calcutta High Court
meta_description: Calcutta HC dismisses Mizoram's appeal against executing a Kolkata land sale cancelled after a new government took office, calling it 'regime revenge'.
bench: Division Bench of Justice Arijit Banerjee and Justice Apurba Sinha Ray
case_name: State of Mizoram and Others v. Excel Vincom Private Limited and Another
citation: Calcutta High Court, Division Bench, order dated 13 November 2026, on appeal from the order dated 2 April 2024 of the Single Judge in Excel Vincom Private Limited & Anr. v. State of Mizoram & Ors.
body: A government guest house on Ashutosh Chowdhury Avenue in Ballygunge, one of Kolkata's more sought-after addresses, has produced a lesson for every state government and public body that sells property through a tender and later has second thoughts. The land had belonged to the Government of Mizoram since 1973. Once Mizoram decided it no longer needed a Kolkata guest house, it floated a tender for the plot's sale, and Excel Vincom Private Limited came out as the successful bidder. The company paid the full sale consideration the tender process called for.

Trouble started after Mizoram went to the polls and the government changed. The new dispensation treated the sale as unfinished business and cancelled it, even though Excel Vincom had already paid in full and, on the Division Bench's own account, had also paid a penalty amount the earlier administration had asked for. Excel Vincom was not content to accept the cancellation and walk away with a refund. It went to the Calcutta High Court seeking enforcement of the sale it believed it had already completed in substance.

A tender for state-owned land, once concluded and paid for, is not supposed to turn into a political football whenever the electorate changes its mind about who runs the state. That is effectively what Excel Vincom argued, and the courts at both levels agreed with it. The company's position was simple: it had done everything the tender asked of it, paid what it was asked to pay, including the penalty, and was entitled to the deed it had bargained for regardless of who sat in the Chief Minister's chair in Aizawl by the time the paperwork was due.

That dispute first reached a Single Judge, Justice Sabyasachi Bhattacharyya, who ruled on 2 April 2024 that Mizoram had to execute a sale deed in Excel Vincom's favour, and gave the state six weeks to do it. Mizoram chose not to comply and instead appealed, arguing among other things that a buyer in Excel Vincom's position should have gone to arbitration or filed a suit for specific performance rather than approach the High Court on its writ side against cancellation of what was, on the state's telling, an essentially contractual sale.

The Division Bench was not persuaded. It upheld the Single Judge's direction and dismissed Mizoram's appeal outright. The reasoning turned on a fact the Bench treated as decisive: the state had already pocketed the entire sale price, and the extra penalty money besides, before it tried to walk back the transaction. Having taken the buyer's money in full and let the sale run its course, a seller, government or private, cannot then use a change in who holds office to reopen a deal it has already closed and been paid for.

On the objection that Excel Vincom should have gone through arbitration or a suit for specific performance instead of a writ petition, the Bench did not accept that this barred the remedy the company had actually sought. Public law remedies against a state authority acting in an arbitrary or unfair manner remain available to a party even where the underlying transaction has a contractual flavour, and the Bench evidently saw little difficulty in Excel Vincom choosing the writ route once the cancellation itself looked arbitrary on its face.

Reports on the ruling describe the Bench as going further and calling the cancellation itself an act of "regime revenge", language that leaves little doubt about how the court viewed a change of government being used to disown a tender process the previous administration had already carried to completion. Courts are usually careful about how far they will go in characterising the motives behind an executive decision, so a Division Bench reaching for language this direct signals how thin it found the state's justification for reopening a sale it had already been paid for in full.

The outcome for Excel Vincom is that it finally gets what it paid for, with the Division Bench ordering Mizoram to execute and register the sale deed within eight weeks. For anyone buying property from a state government, a public sector undertaking, or any public authority through a tender, the ruling is a reminder that payment of the full consideration, accepted without protest by the seller, tends to close off any later argument that the sale can simply be undone because the people running the seller have changed. A change of government is a political fact. It is not, on this ruling, a reason in law to unwind a concluded sale.
why_it_matters: Buyers who acquire property from state governments or public bodies through a tender often worry about a change in administration unsettling a deal already paid for. This ruling tells such buyers, including corporate and high-value purchasers negotiating with public authorities, that full payment accepted by the seller closes off a later attempt to cancel on political grounds, and that courts will look past procedural objections to protect a buyer who has already performed its side of the bargain.
card_summary: Calcutta High Court dismisses Mizoram's appeal against executing a Kolkata land sale cancelled after a change of government, calling the cancellation 'regime revenge' since the state had already taken full payment.
card_tip: Once a state or public body accepts full payment under a concluded tender sale, a later change of government is not, on this ruling, a ground to cancel it.
